Paying off high interest loan first analogy?

Maybe something like having a bunch of holes in a boat. You keep scooping up water with a bucket and throwing it back overboard and your girlfriend is the one that is trying to plug the holes. The boat is sinking fast and, despite using the bucket, the boat is beginning to sink. Your girlfriend wants to focus on this one particular hole in the front of the boat. This hole is leaking a tiny bit but is the result of rotten wood. The whole front end is rotten in fact; it looks terrible. It's so disgusting and rotten that water is beginning to seep in through that rotten wood. On the back of the boat is another hole. This hole is just drilled into the boat with a huge 2" drill bit. The back of the boat is freshly painted and there isn't any rotten wood, but the painter decided to drill that huge hole into the boat before throwing you guys into the water.

You guys are trying not to sink. You shouldn't care about what is causing the leaks in the boat, you need to seal them up. Even though the front of the boat looks worse, it isn't letting as much water in as the hole in the back of the boat, even though the hole in that area appears to be less problematic.

This is cheating a little because it's not explaining to her why it works, but since people often respond to visuals... give http://unbury.me/ a try.

On unbury.me you type in the loans' information, then you can toggle back and forth between "avalanche" and "snowball" to see what difference the high-interest-loan-first approach ("avalanche") makes.

A couple of thoughts:

1) Split the loans into equals amounts: if you have a $500 loan @ 8% interest and $1500 @ 4% interest, imagine it as 4 separate loans: $500@8%, $500@4%, $500@4%, $500@4% - which one(s) should you pay off first?

2) Imagine all the loans are owed to the same person and that person is you, i.e. someone owes you $500@8% and $1500@4%. Which loans would you want to debtor to keep open the longest vs which loans would you not want to debtor to pay first? As the debtor, do the opposite of what's best for the creditor.

All that said, if the snowball method gives a psychological motivational boost to keep spirits up and keep paying down the debt, then use the snowball method.

Curious- what do you mean by "use their own certs"? What would they be signing?

When you implement a filtering system nearer the the router, you have to strip HTTPS and reapply it between your network hardware and the destination machine. This requires having a cert that is manually trusted by machines inside the network and increased processing load on your network hardware.

It adds the ability to snoop secure network traffic, monitor what your employees are doing, etc. There are additional privacy, security, resource and personnel requirements, so while it works at the corporate level it makes a lot more sense to distribute the processing load and keep website security intact in this environment via adblocking software at the browser.
